pages.text: It was the last week of Form 3. The corridors felt different, quieter and louder at once. Teachers smiled more than usual. In a few days, the Basic Education Certificate Examination would begin. “It feels like the end of the world,” said Harriet. “It is the end of a chapter,” said Mr Anan, the form master, “not the end of the story.”

pages.alt: Students stand in a quiet corridor with posters on the wall and the form master smiling.

pages.text: Mr Anan gave the class a checklist for exam day. “Check your index number the night before. Pack two blue or black pens, a pencil, an eraser, a ruler and a mathematical set. Sleep early. Eat breakfast. Arrive early. Switch off and hand in anything the rules say you may not carry. And breathe.” Clement wrote it all down. He wrote “breathe” in capitals.

pages.text: The night before, Harriet checked her examination slip three times. Clement packed his bag, unpacked it and packed it again. His younger sister watched, amused. “You are nervous,” she said. “A little,” said Clement. “A lot.” She handed him a drink and a biscuit. “Do your best,” she said. “That is all anybody can ask.”

pages.text: On the first morning, Clement arrived early. The hall was quiet, the desks neat. He sat with his pen in hand as the invigilator read the instructions. “Read every question carefully,” said the invigilator. “Plan your time. Write your index number on every sheet. When time is called, stop writing.” Clement’s heart pounded. Then he opened the paper, took a breath and began.

pages.text: On the last day of the exams, the students poured out of the hall in a wave of laughter and relief. Someone pulled out a felt pen. Soon every white shirt was covered in messages: “Good luck!”, “Never forget us”, “Best of friends”. Mr Anan reminded them: “Write kind words only. A memory should make people smile.” Clement’s shirt filled with names, and his eyes grew misty.

pages.text: Clement and Harriet went back to the classroom to find Mr Anan. The chalkboard still read “Good luck, Form 3.” “Thank you, sir,” said Harriet. “You taught us more than lessons.” Mr Anan wiped his glasses. “You taught me too,” he said. “Whatever your results, remember this: you are more than a score.” Harriet smiled. “We will visit,” she said. “Please do,” he said.

pages.text: That evening, Clement wrote to Mr Anan. Because his teacher was an older person he knew, he wrote a semi-formal letter, with his address and the date at the top. “House 5, Forest Road, Techiman. 18th June, 2027. Dear Mr Anan, I hope you are well. I am writing to thank you for everything you have done for our class. You taught us to read, to reason and to believe in ourselves. I will always remember your kindness and your patience. I hope to visit the school when I begin senior high school. Yours sincerely, Clement Duodu.”

Dear Mr Anan, I hope you are well.
I am writing to thank you for everything you have done for our class.
You taught us to read, to reason and to believe in ourselves.
I will always remember your kindness and your patience.
I hope to visit the school when I begin senior high school.
Yours sincerely, Clement Duodu.”
pages.alt: A boy writes a thank-you letter at a desk with his signed white shirt folded beside him.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a farewell letter can mix warm feeling with polite language. Clement used “Dear Mr Anan” and “Yours sincerely”, because he knew the name, and he gave a specific reason to thank his teacher. He wrote “thank you” and “I will always remember”, not “thx” or “miss u”. Good luck to every Form 3 learner. The end.
